lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Sichuan Small Towns Development Project, P110632. Loan IBRD-80420 of US$100 million, approved 10 May 2011 and effective 28 September 2011, restructured 29 January 2016, closed on its original date of 31 December 2016. US$93.32 million was disbursed according to the completion report's data sheet and US$93,574,827.58 according to the Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet. Total project cost at appraisal was US$169.95 million. Environmental category B. The implementing agency was the Sichuan Provincial Project Management Office. The completion report of 31 May 2017 rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to the development outcome Moderate, and Bank performance and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gave the same four ratings, except that its table prints the completion report's risk rating as Modest, which is not the word the report uses (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 May 2017; IEG ICR Review ICRR0020788, 4 December 2017).

companies.role: Provincial project office that ran the loan; the completion report records that it was short of staff at the start of implementation because almost all its capacity was going to another Bank project
companies.desc: The provincial-level office set up to run this World Bank loan for the Sichuan provincial government, with a project management office and implementation unit in each of the eight project towns. The completion report records no activity for it outside Bank-financed work.

cases.community: The project widened and rebuilt roads, water and sewerage networks, canals and river embankments in eight towns in Sichuan. The completion report gives the outcome: land acquisition took 2,387.32 mu of collective land and 526.95 mu of state-owned land, affecting 2,802 households or 8,720 people; houses measuring 142,192.3 were demolished, affecting 605 households against 528 households estimated in the resettlement plans - the report's text gives that figure in cubic metres and its own table in square metres; and structures measuring 39,867.25 belonging to 34 enterprises or other entities were demolished. Separately, works added in Liujiang Town in 2015 took 19.7 mu of land from 19 households, 83 people, in Yang Village and Lianghe Village. The report then records what had not happened. By the time the loan closed on 31 December 2016, 348 households in four counties and districts had still not been resettled: 148 in Xinjin, 54 in Miyi, 80 in Zizhong and 66 in Jialing. The report gives the reason: the resettlement houses for this project were only a small part of large resettlement sites that local governments were building for displaced people from this and other domestic projects, construction of those sites was delayed, and their implementation was not under the control of the Bank's project. A supplementary resettlement plan was agreed between Sichuan and the Bank, with commitment letters from local governments and willingness letters from households, under which most of the remaining households were to be allocated houses by March 2017 and to get their keys by September 2017. By the completion mission at the end of March 2017, three months after the loan closed, 114 households in Zizhong and Jialing had still not been resettled. The report records that the completion mission was informed that households in those two counties changed their minds and did not take the county government's offer of an existing resettlement site, deciding to wait for the originally planned housing, which is closer to where they had lived, while continuing to draw monthly transition subsidies of 240 yuan a person in Zizhong; 25 households in Jialing District had signed a willingness letter in December 2016 to wait until the end of 2018. The report's own schedule shows 38 households in Jialing not due to be resettled until December 2018 and 58 households in Zizhong not until June 2018, two years after the loan closed. The report also states that compensation was paid in compliance with Chinese regulations and Bank policy, that in some cases extra government budget was provided to raise compensation to replacement cost at the time of implementation rather than the standard set in the plan years earlier, that external monitoring found the income of affected residents higher than before the project, and that no complaints were received throughout the project.
cases.displaced_label: households whose houses were demolished, against 528 estimated in the resettlement plans; 2,802 households or 8,720 people were affected by land acquisition (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,119 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 2,802 households or 8,720 people affected by land acquisition and 605 households whose houses were demolished. No figure matching 6,119 appears in the completion report, in the Independent Evaluation Group's review or in the appraisal document, and the documents do not explain the gap. ICIJ’s own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank’s documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts", and it says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement action plans, which are written before the work is done, and looked to completion reports where no resettlement document existed. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2016 with 348 households not yet resettled, and 114 of them were still not resettled three months later. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the risk that the remaining resettlement would be further delayed or not completed as Substantial. For what happened after that, the review has no document: it states that the project team told it by email on 29 October 2017 that as of September 2017 agreements had been signed for house distribution in Xinjin and Miyi, that houses for 14 households in Jialing were to be completed by October 2017 and for 4 more by December 2017, that houses for 38 households in Jialing were to be delivered by December 2018, and that construction for 58 households in Zizhong was to start in October 2017 with houses ready by June 2018. The Bank's filing for the project ends with that review and a 2017 audit report, and neither records whether those dates were met.

cases.community: Two years into implementation, 588 houses in a 13-hectare area around the Gupan Pond in the Ming Old City of Qufu were demolished in 44 days, except for five buildings designated as historic. The completion report states that neither China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage, nor the World Bank, nor UNESCO was informed about the planned demolition. The site sits inside the buffer zone of the Temple and Cemetery of Confucius and the Kong Family Mansion World Heritage Site. The completion report records the clearance as one major incident of non-compliance with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, and its lessons section says the non-compliance was found when the local implementation unit moved ahead with resettling residents at the Gupan Pond without an approved resettlement plan. The subproject was also out of compliance with UNESCO's buffer-zone requirements for World Heritage sites and was cancelled at the restructuring of April 2016, although the Bank kept the resettlement linked to the project. UNESCO's World Heritage Centre wrote to China on 9 December 2013 about the razing of the housing; China replied on 28 March 2014, describing the work as a comprehensive renovation project partly funded by the World Bank, covering 13.34 hectares of the buffer zone, and stating that 588 households had been moved since the first half of 2013. The World Heritage Committee's decision 38 COM 7B.11 of 2014 noted the redevelopment and expressed concern about its potential impact on the site's Outstanding Universal Value, including its authenticity and integrity. An ICOMOS reactive monitoring mission visited from 9 to 12 December 2014. The next state-of-conservation report, considered in 2016 under decision 40 COM 7B.32, records that the 13.34-hectare area had held 588 households, that most of the housing had been built after the 1970s and about a third of it was dilapidated, that five buildings were found historically valuable and saved, and that no construction had followed the demolition, and that the suspension of the reconstruction project had a negative impact on the public credibility of the local government. Across the whole project the completion report counts 790 households resettled - 588 in Qufu and 202 in Zoucheng - affecting 3,612 people. The resettlement plans had estimated demolition of urban housing belonging to 346 households, 1,211 people, in Qufu and 342 households, 1,198 people, in Zoucheng. In Qufu 86,300 square metres of urban housing was demolished against 40,524 planned, and 206.5 mu of state-owned land was permanently occupied against 94.3 mu planned. In Zoucheng 33,274.86 square metres of urban housing and 2,051.88 square metres of rural housing were demolished, affecting 190 households, 760 people, and 12 households, 52 people. Across both cities 204 shops were demolished, affecting 1,014 people. Unlicensed buildings were also taken: 194 households, 692 people, in Qufu and 78 households, 213 people, in Zoucheng. Resettlement cost 492.63 million yuan in Qufu and 178.83 million yuan in Zoucheng. The completion report also says that at the start of implementation project activities were largely decided without sufficient consultation with local communities, and that a social development team was later commissioned on the Bank team's recommendation to run public consultation. On the Gupan Pond site itself the report says the Bank task team took on the management of the resettlement after the subproject was dropped, that all affected households received resettlement houses before the loan closed, that the resettlement compound was about 500 metres from the original houses, that families moving there came from the same neighbourhood and kept their community ties, that the new housing had solar panels, heating, parking and storage, and that house values in the area rose from about 3,000 to 5,600 yuan a square metre after the resettlement began.

cases.confidence_note: The demolition is recorded outside the Bank. UNESCO's World Heritage Centre raised it with China in December 2013, the World Heritage Committee addressed it in two decisions, and an ICOMOS reactive monitoring mission visited the site in December 2014. That is why this is not rated as resting on the lender alone. Two limits on the independent record: the figure of 588 households moved is China's own statement to UNESCO, not a finding by UNESCO; and UNESCO's concern is about the World Heritage site, not about the people who were moved. On the people, the Bank's completion report is the only source. It is the lender reporting on its own project, and it contains both the non-compliance finding and a favourable account of the destination housing, the distance moved and the rise in local house prices. No independent press report, field study or court record about the households themselves was found; searches in English and in Chinese returned only World Bank and UNESCO documents. The completion report's own figures do not fully line up: its summary says 588 households were resettled in Qufu, while its lessons section refers to 251 households having originally lived at the Gupan Pond, and no document explains the difference. The Independent Evaluation Group's review carries no date on the document itself; the date given is the one in the Bank's own document-system record for it.
cases.conditions: The loan was environmental category B and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement action plan was prepared before approval and disclosed locally and at the Bank's InfoShop in November 2010; an abbreviated plan for activities added at restructuring was disclosed locally in July 2015 and at the InfoShop in December 2015. An external monitoring team reported on compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy twice a year, and a further contract for external monitoring of resettlement in Qufu was added to the project at restructuring. The Gupan Pond clearance went ahead before a resettlement plan for it had been approved, which the completion report records as a major incident of non-compliance with that policy; the site also fell under UNESCO's buffer-zone requirements for World Heritage sites, which the completion report says the demolition did not meet. After the subcomponent was cancelled the Bank kept the resettlement linked to the project and the Bank task team took over its management, communicating directly with UNESCO and the State Administration of Cultural Heritage on a revised urban design (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 December 2017).

cases.community: The project built about 20 kilometres of primary and secondary roads in the Panggong area of Xiangcheng District, which the completion report describes as formerly a rural area with rural roads and streets, together with a bus corridor and terminal on Route 13 and traffic management works. The completion report gives the outcome of the land acquisition: at project closing all 776 families affected by land acquisition had been compensated and 768 families had been resettled. The number of people to be resettled rose above the original estimate because the city's master plan changed and because households that had been surveyed voluntarily split into more households. The report records what went wrong. The mid-term review of May 2015 named resettlement as the critical issue. Funds for land acquisition were secured, but funds were not available for the resettlement housing; despite an agreement at the mid-term review to meet targets by October 2015, work on the resettlement housing started only in 2016 and some of it was finished only in 2017. Because the housing was late, construction of some of the roads in Panggong was delayed by more than two years, and the project's closing date had to be extended twice, from September 2017 to July 2019. The report names the cause as a lack of coordination between three bodies: the project management office, responsible for road construction; the Xiangcheng District Government, responsible for land acquisition; and the Xiangcheng Urban Investment Company, responsible for building the resettlement housing. All three were committed to the work, the report says, but their plans and priorities were not coordinated in time. The municipal government changed the compensation process in 2015 and introduced cash compensation as an alternative in order to speed matters up, and the Bank's social specialist made a separate support mission in December 2017 to deal with resettlement issues. The report also records the other side. It says resettlement was an opportunity for some families to improve their housing significantly, that housing visited by the completion mission appeared to be of satisfactory quality, that the residents met expressed satisfaction with their new homes, and that no resettlement-related complaints were received during the project. Household surveys by the social safeguard monitoring consultant found the average annual income of the sampled affected households rose from RMB 28,000 in 2012 to RMB 44,000 in 2018, an annual rate of 11.5 per cent, which the report says is more than the growth of Xiangyang's gross domestic product, and that the value of the assets those households owned after resettlement, mainly housing, was about four to five times what it had been before. The report adds that unfavourable customary practices for women on resettlement existed in the project area, so that without the project women might not have had access to information or the same level of compensation as men, and that women made up half the participants in the local resettlement meetings.

cases.community: The project built six wastewater treatment plants and rehabilitated three rivers in Nanning. The completion report compares plan with outcome: 1,577 households, 7,130 people, were planned to be affected and 1,904 households, 7,968 people, actually were; permanent and temporary land acquisition planned at 2,175.19 and 733.1 mu came to 2,687.073 mu; and 4,428.86 square metres of houses and 89,696.84 square metres of other structures were demolished against 34,871 square metres of structures planned. The report records two things left unfinished. First, four village groups in Nanxiang Village - Nos. 1, 2, 9 and 11 - had not received the official certificate for the commercial land they had been granted; their land acquisition and compensation agreements were signed with the resettlement office of the Jiangnan District Government. Group No. 1 got its certificate by December 2016; Groups Nos. 2 and 9 were expected to receive theirs by December 2017 and Group No. 11 by December 2018, two and a half years after the loan closed. The report says the certificates were delayed because the documents the groups submitted were incomplete, and says elsewhere that all the compensation is completed and that the issuance of the remaining certificates is a matter of time because the necessary documents have since been submitted by the village groups. The project office agreed in an official letter of 10 April 2017 to keep working with the Jiangnan District Government on the issue and to report to the Bank every six months until the certificates were issued. cases.community: The project built sewers, water treatment and solid waste facilities in Shanghai. The resettlement plans at appraisal identified 1,112 project-affected people in 282 households, with 697.65 mu, 46 hectares, of compulsory land acquisition and 60 commercial enterprises to be affected or relocated. The completion report gives the outcome: 598.5 mu, 40 hectares, was actually acquired; 174 people in 44 households were affected; and 10 commercial enterprises were affected or relocated. Most of the reduction came from a change in construction method on the Western Trunk Sewer, where pipe-jacking replaced open-trench work in heavily built-up downtown areas, so that component moved nobody at all against a plan of 1,064 people in 266 households. The five subprojects financed through the district facility ran the other way: they moved 174 people in 44 households against a plan of 48 people in 16 households, and took 587 mu of land against 442 planned. Compensation for land acquisition, demolition of structures and resettlement came to RMB 188.26 million against RMB 448 million estimated at appraisal. Independent monitoring confirmed that the full compensation set out in each resettlement plan was paid; the final external monitoring report found all resettlement had followed the plans with no outstanding issues. Post-construction surveys by the independent monitoring consultant of every subproject where resettlement occurred found no instance of a negative impact on the area around the affected people, that compensation was paid in every case for land acquisition and resettlement, and that rural households were paid for losses on farming and crop plantings. Rural affected people were offered retraining through local village committees to make a living by other means, and the report says those who took it were very satisfied with the improvement in their living standards and household income. There was no appeal during construction, and the report says no ethnic minorities or vulnerable groups were affected. One component was dropped partly because of people living on the site: the closure of the Minhang solid waste dump was cancelled at the restructuring of March 2014, and one of the three reasons the report gives is illegal encroachment at the site involving a large building and a large area planted with valuable commercial trees, so that going ahead would have triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy and cost more time to prepare the safeguard documents. The borrower said it would complete the closures with its own money and continue a five-year independent environmental monitoring programme of the sites.

cases.community: The project built wastewater collection and treatment, public toilets, solid waste transfer and industrial wastewater pollution control works in Liuzhou. The completion report sets plan against outcome component by component. In the wastewater component 510,756 square metres of land was acquired against 519,340 planned, 50,245 square metres of housing was demolished against 54,128, 72 enterprises were affected against 76, and 2,254 people were affected against 3,858; compensation cost RMB 214,276,671 against RMB 181,537,705 planned, an increase the report attributes to higher compensation standards. In the municipal sanitation component 9,034 square metres of land was acquired against 10,007 planned and 2,573 square metres of housing was demolished against 11,992, with no enterprises or people recorded as affected; compensation cost RMB 12,560,271 against RMB 28,955,685 planned, the fall attributed to the partial cancellation of the public toilets. The solid waste transfer station took 25,310 square metres against 23,856 planned, with no demolition and no affected persons, at a compensation cost of RMB 9,698,846 against RMB 4,506,138. All 42 community solid waste collection stations were cancelled, so the 3,318 square metres of land and the RMB 996,984 planned for them were not needed. Across the project 545,100 square metres of land was acquired against 556,521 planned, 52,818 square metres of housing was demolished against 66,120, 72 enterprises were affected against 76, 2,254 people were affected against 3,858, and total compensation came to RMB 236,535,788 against RMB 215,996,512. The report says resettlement was carried out satisfactorily and all affected people resettled in accordance with the agreed resettlement plan, that the compensation standards actually applied for land acquisition and house demolition were higher than those in the plan, that all compensation payments were made on time, that all affected people were fully consulted and that their incomes were restored. The compensation funds were distributed to the affected households because no land was redistributed, and livelihoods were restored by setting up collective-owned businesses and job placement assistance. Resettlement practice for the wastewater and sanitation components was monitored by the Shanghai Academy of Social Science, which reported to the Bank every six months and completed its resettlement completion reports in March 2011. Its sample income survey found the average annual family income of the households investigated was RMB 12,900 before resettlement and RMB 13,330 after, and that residential conditions had improved to some degree, with housing changing from mostly timber-brick to cement-brick and gas, telephone and sewerage installed. Special financial assistance, special housing arrangements and labour assistance were provided on request to vulnerable affected people - widows, elderly people, disabled people and children. Siting was changed twice to cut the resettlement: 62 public toilets were planned, but most of the sites chosen were in densely populated areas needing a large amount of land acquisition and considerable resettlement, so after work with the city planning bureau and land department the sites were moved to public and empty land and the number cut: the Bank's section of the report records 42 public toilets and 30 portable toilets built, and the borrower's section 43 public toilets, 30 portable toilets and two mobile toilets; and the 42 community solid waste collection stations were dropped after opposition to their placement in the communities, with existing stations upgraded instead.

cases.community: The railway took 14,867 mu of land, 57 per cent of it farmland. The completion report states that the land acquisition affected 7,416 households in 116 villages, 10 counties and districts and 29 townships across three municipalities, Hohhot and Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia and Zhangjiakou City in Hebei. It resulted in the demolition of 396,969 square metres of houses and the relocation of 1,446 households. A further 168 enterprises, with 1,879 employees, were affected, and 6,717 mu of land was temporarily occupied and restored after construction. Compensation agreements for land were signed between the county or city land resources bureau and the affected villages, with funds paid to the villages through townships and sub-districts; agreements for houses were signed with each household and paid directly. As of the closing date of 30 June 2020, compensation of RMB 2,156 million, about US$317 million, had been paid in full in Inner Mongolia, and 96 per cent of the RMB 1,664 million, about US$245 million, due in Hebei had been paid. Overall 97 per cent of the project's compensation had been paid and RMB 67 million in Hebei had not. The report gives two reasons, and gives the funding shortage as RMB 57 million in the sentence that introduces them and as RMB 56 million in the bullet that follows. Zhangjiakou Municipality had a funding gap of RMB 56 million for state-owned land, collectively owned land and water wells; the municipal government directed Wanquan District and Huai'an County to borrow RMB 30 million each from Zhangjiakou Bank to cover it, its wholly owned financing vehicle Zhangjiakou Transport Investment Company issued a letter of commitment, and the loan applications had started. Separately three households declined the compensation offered under the resettlement plan. The funds, based on a third-party evaluation, were held in escrow for them, the Wanquan District Government had retained replacement apartments of around 100 square metres each, several rounds of negotiation failed to reach agreement, and the report adds that the three households have houses or apartments elsewhere to live in. Three enterprises in Huai'an County also declined the compensation offered and two filed lawsuits; their funds were also in escrow, and the county government undertook to follow the court's directive if it set different amounts. The report says the Bank would continue to supervise these issues until they were fully addressed. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that its discussion with the Bank task team showed the team was still following up with the borrower on the outstanding resettlement compensation payments more than a year after the project closed; that is a statement by Bank staff to the evaluators, not a document.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2020 with 97 per cent of compensation paid and RMB 67 million outstanding in Hebei Province, covering a municipal funding shortfall of RMB 56 million and unresolved disputes with three households and three enterprises, two of which had gone to court. The two Bank documents disagree on the project's outcome: the completion report of 30 June 2021 rated it Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group's review rated it Moderately Unsatisfactory.

When the report was drafted in December 2018 the 68 in Huaibei and 284 in Lu'an had been resettled, and 121 households in Lu'an had still not been relocated to permanent housing: 65 were expected to move in August 2019 and 56 in 2020. On compensation the report says the external monitoring consultant found the transition subsidy was paid in conformity with local policy, that the affected people were compensated in time to rehabilitate their livelihoods, that the transitional support was paid twice over because the transitional period was extended, and that on local leasing market information the subsidy the remaining 121 households received was well sufficient to pay rent for housing similar to their original property. lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Second National Railways Project (Zhe-Gan Line), P075602. Loan IBRD-47460 of US$200 million, approved 24 June 2004, effective 16 January 2005, closed 31 January 2008 on the original closing date, with US$199.0 million disbursed. Environmental category A. The completion report, ICR0000918, is dated 15 August 2008 on its cover and 17 August 2008 in its own data sheet. It rated the outcome Satisfactory, risk to the development outcome Low or Negligible, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Highly Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, ICRR13032, posted 30 September 2008, gave the same outcome, risk, Bank performance and borrower performance ratings. The review rated the quality of the completion report Satisfactory while noting that the report "does not discuss the number of people resettled".

companies.name: Ministry of Railways, Foreign Capital and Technical Import Center
companies.role: The unit inside China's then Ministry of Railways that handled foreign-financed railway projects, named in the completion report as the implementing agency and abbreviated FCTIC. The report records that the ministry did not administer resettlement itself: that was done by local governments from the provincial level down to the village level, and the ministry's centre intervened when resettlement was delayed.

cases.community: The project raised speeds, renewed signalling and electrified the double-track Zhe-Gan line, and realigning the track shortened it from 942 to 916 kilometres. Annex 2 of the completion report sets the appraisal plan against the outcome. Land acquisition was planned at 26,668 mu and came to 31,800 mu. Resettlement was planned for 2,666 families and came to 7,573 families, nearly three times the plan. At appraisal the resettlement plan covered 560 villages in 133 townships in three provinces along 943 kilometres of line, and the appraisal document states that the project would affect 49,102 people, including 45,853 affected by land requisition and 2,666 households with 9,401 inhabitants subject to structure demolition, with 6,152 people affected by both. The report's own account of the resettlement is favourable: a completion mission visited five resettlement villages in five different counties in March 2008 and, after talking to resettled people, resettlement staff and local officials, concluded the resettlement had been completed successfully and that the affected people were satisfied with their compensation and other arrangements. Resettlement was monitored by Southwest Communication University, and people were compensated by redistribution of land, by an alternative site or in cash. The report also records that there were a few delays in resettlement caused by the administrative structure, in which the ministry pays and local government administers, and gives as a lesson that "On China railway projects this can lead to a disconnect between the project's Resettlement Action Plan and actual implementation." Neither Bank document explains why the number of families resettled came out at 7,573 against a plan of 2,666, and neither names a village where people moved.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on time on 31 January 2008 with the railway built. The completion report records 7,573 families resettled against 2,666 planned, and 31,800 mu of land taken against 26,668 mu planned, without accounting for the gap. The Independent Evaluation Group agreed with every rating the report gave and, in the same review, recorded as a shortcoming that the report does not discuss the number of people resettled, although Annex 2 of the report gives the number of families.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: China: Nanchang Urban Rail Project, P132154. Loan IBRD-82620 (Loan 8262-CN), approved 20 June 2013 at US$250 million, effective 21 October 2013, mid-term review 13 February 2017, restructured 17 August 2018, original closing 31 October 2018, actual closing 31 December 2019. The loan was cut to US$189,492,846, all of which was disbursed. Total project cost was US$2,189,961,846 at completion against US$2,571,230,000 at appraisal. Environmental category A. The loan triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment (OP/BP 4.01), physical cultural resources (OP 4.11) and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). A separate project component covered land acquisition and resettlement costs, financed entirely by the client and not by the Bank. The completion report of 31 December 2020 rated the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and M&E quality Substantial. companies.name: Nanchang Urban Rail Group Co.
companies.role: Named in the completion report data sheet as the implementing agency and in its text as the URC. It prepared and carried out the resettlement plan, which was disclosed at its offices in January 2013, and the report records that it went on to apply the Bank's compensation and resettlement approach to the city's Lines 3 and 4. The completion report also records that it failed to coordinate utility relocation and traffic diversion effectively, which contributed to the delay in the works.

cases.community: Clearing the Line 2 corridor required demolition of housing and of commercial premises. The completion report states that resettlement work started in April 2013, that the demolition of private houses and the resettlement work connected with it was fully completed by August 2014, and that the enterprise structures were finished by the end of 2017. It then states: "Altogether 1344 urban families, 130 enterprises and 41 rural families were affected and 170,468.13m2 of land was acquired." The report says cash compensation and resettlement relocation housing were provided to the displaced families, and that 27 per cent of the affected families gained an improvement in their living environment; it gives no figure for the other families. Implementing the resettlement plan cost US$514 million, more than twice the US$193 million estimated at appraisal, and was funded entirely by the client. The report records that the final Bank supervision mission concluded the social safeguards were satisfactory, that nine external monitoring reports confirm the affected people were satisfied with the process, and that the relocation of the No. 28 High School was chosen as best practice for the Bank's Urban Rail Handbook for the measures taken to limit disruption to commuting and classroom schedules. At appraisal the figures were different and larger: acquisition of 746 mu of village land, 259 mu of it cultivated, affecting 142 people from 31 families; demolition of 83,817 square metres of structures owned by 1,043 families and affecting 4,001 people; and demolition of 201 shops and 22 enterprises and organisations. Neither document compares the appraisal count of 1,043 families with the completion count of 1,344 urban families and 41 rural families, and neither says how many of the 1,344 lost their homes as against their land. Resettlement of commercial entities along Line 2 was one of the reasons the closing date had to be extended.
cases.outcome: Line 2 opened and the loan closed on 31 December 2019. The demolition of private houses was completed by August 2014 and the demolition of enterprise structures by the end of 2017, and 170,468.13 square metres of land was acquired. The completion report of 31 December 2020 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 May 2021 both rate the project Satisfactory and both treat the resettlement as satisfactory; the review cuts the M&E rating to Modest.

ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count: it looked for what Bank documents call project-affected people, searching them for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced"; where a document counted only households it looked up an average household size; it decided to include all impacts, temporary ones among them, and says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement plans written before the work was done. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.

The completion report, ICR00002898, is dated 24 December 2013 on its cover and 14 November 2013 in its own data sheet; it rated the outcome Unsatisfactory, risk to the development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and rated the resettlement moderately satisfactory. companies.role: External resettlement monitor, contracted by the provincial project office in 2007. cases.community: Land was taken in the suburbs of county towns to build water plants and wells. The completion report states that resettlement activities were carried out moderately satisfactorily, that a final report on resettlement implementation was prepared, "but there are inconsistencies in the data, which the PPMO has not been able to clarify." It gives the actual impacts as almost 660 mu of permanently acquired land, which affected 713 households or 2,834 people, and 300 square metres of residential housing demolition, which affected 4 households or 15 people. Annex 5 of the report sets out the 713 households and 2,834 people subproject by subproject across 20 water supply schemes, the largest being Lushan with 130 households and 520 people and Dengzhou with 87 households and 348 people, and totals 659.73 mu. Table 5.2 of the same annex, comparing planned with actual, gives the number of affected people as 1,041, not 2,834, and the actual permanent land acquisition as 644.95 mu, not 659.73; neither document reconciles either pair. On compensation the report says the rates for resettlement and land acquisition ended up higher than the rates agreed in the resettlement plan, "except for about 57.4 mu of land for which an annual rental fee is being paid". Land was also used temporarily to lay water pipes, mostly along main urban roads and returned to its owners shortly after installation, and farmers whose crops were affected were compensated under local government rules. The cost of land acquisition and resettlement fell from an estimate of RMB 97.67 million to about RMB 34.67 million, which the report attributes to subprojects in 17 participating counties being dropped from the project; Annex 5 gives the final figure as RMB 36.47 million. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the report's resettlement account but leaves out the 57.4 mu paid for by annual rent, and so states without qualification that the compensation rates ended up higher than the rates agreed in the plan.

About 57.4 mu of land was still being paid for by an annual rental fee rather than compensated at the agreed rate when the report was written. The Independent Evaluation Group downgraded borrower performance to Unsatisfactory.

It also records that resettlement was slow: in some densely populated areas additional resettlement was needed, which delayed some road construction and rehabilitation, resettlement was rated moderately satisfactory around the mid-term review because of slow progress in building the resettlement site, and resettlement was eventually completed on time. An Ethnic Minority Development Plan was prepared, the appraisal document having recorded that ethnic minorities make up about 65 per cent of Yining city's population and Uygurs 49.7 per cent, and the report says it was implemented as planned. The appraisal document had set out 980 mu of land to be taken from 13 villages affecting 922 people in 213 households, 2,837 people in 648 households to be relocated by house demolition, and 130 shops or vendors and 21 enterprises and institutes to be affected.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2017 with 93 households' houses demolished, about a seventh of the 648 planned, and land taken from 166 households. Both Bank documents rate the project and its resettlement satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group recorded that the money spent on land acquisition and compensation cannot be traced in the appraisal document, the loan agreement or the completion report.

cases.community: The project dredged and widened about 205.6 kilometres of the Shaying River channel for navigation, strengthened 43.87 kilometres of bank, rebuilt four bridges and added ship locks. The completion report states that by project closure all resettlement was complete except for one outstanding issue at Sanba village in Yingshang county, where 23 rural households had been resettled. In January 2018, after the loan closed, the Bank was informed that a large area of Sanba village, including the Sanba resettlement site itself, had been identified by the county government for economic development and that the 23 households would be moved to another site. Ten of the 23 took cash compensation and left. The remaining 13 chose to move to Xiayuan Resident Compound, a new site assigned by Yingshang county government, where construction was expected to be finished only by June 2019. Those 13 households were given an 18-month transition fee, which the report says is sufficient to rent houses in nearby towns. The report says the Bank remained committed to their satisfactory resettlement in compliance with Bank policy, that the provincial project office agreed to go on monitoring it under a later Bank-supported programme covering Fuyang municipality, that Yingshang County would provide six-monthly interim reports on the progress of the resettlement housing, that a grievance mechanism was being established so the 13 households could raise concerns with the provincial office, and that Bank social specialists would visit in early 2019 and June 2019. The report also records that land acquisition was delayed by weak coordination between the county land bureaus and the project company and by delays in agreeing the unit price for land compensation, and that new resettlement plans were prepared when additional land was required. On the wider picture it says the livelihoods of resettled households had been improved to a certain extent and that resettled households said the new bridge made their lives and travel more convenient. At appraisal the project was to take 1,658 mu, 111 hectares, permanently and 9,874 mu, 658 hectares, temporarily, to relocate 364 households involving 1,489 people, and to affect 2,891 households, 10,316 people, through temporary land use at 34 sites for dredged sediment, for a stated total of 3,679 households, 13,456 people, affected by resettlement. Neither Bank document gives an outcome count of households relocated across the whole project.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2017. A month later the Bank learned that the resettlement site built for the 23 Sanba village households had been designated by the county government for economic development, so the households had to move a second time. Ten took cash and left. Thirteen were renting housing in nearby towns on an 18-month transition fee, waiting for a new compound that was not expected to be finished before June 2019, about 18 months after the loan closed. Monitoring of their resettlement was transferred to a later Bank-financed programme. No document found records whether the 13 households moved in.

cases.community: The project built roads, water supply and village infrastructure across several counties and districts of Chongqing. The clearest recorded failure is in Tongliang. The borrower's account in Annex 7 of the completion report states that in Tongliang, because of complicated procedures and the land quota set by the state government, land for the road construction was initially compensated as a land lease; this was finally corrected to the Bank's requirements and all the villages and villagers were properly compensated for the land acquired under Bank policies. The report's assessment of Bank supervision records the timing: some issues stayed unresolved for a protracted period, among them the "resettlement issue in Tongliang, solved just at the loan closing although the works had been completed three years earlier." The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats that the resettlement issue in Tongliang was solved at loan closing. On scale the report's body text and its own annex do not agree. The body text gives the actual resettlement impacts as 412.526 mu of permanently acquired land, which affected 593 households or 2,837 people, and 70 square metres of residential housing demolished, which affected seven houses and 25 people. Annex 7's table instead gives 309.194 mu acquired case by case, 322.526 mu acquired permanently and 90 mu allocated by government; 2,474.96 square metres of house demolition with 593 affected households and 2,387 project-affected people; and, in a separate column, seven impacted individual enterprises covering 70 square metres with 25 project-affected people. So the 70 square metres and the 25 people that the body text attributes to seven houses are, in the annex, seven enterprises, and the annex's figure of 2,387 people differs from the body text's 2,837 by a transposed pair of digits. Neither document explains either difference. The subprojects in the annex are the Yongchun roads, with 1,810 square metres demolished, 203 affected households and 899 people, the Tongliang roads with 52 households and 144 people, Qijiang New Countryside with 153 households and 602 people, and in Chengkou the water supply with 2 households and 10 people and the roads with 664.96 square metres, 183 households and 732 people. On the other side of the ledger the report says the compensation rates for resettlement and land acquisition exceeded the rates agreed in the resettlement plan, that compensation to each affected household was increased because land prices had risen and more favourable compensation policies had been issued, that compensation funds were issued without delay or deduction, that the independent monitoring consultant's survey found no project-affected people were pushed into poverty by the land acquisition and that for most of them incomes and living conditions improved, and that external monitoring reported the resettlement plan had limited impact on household incomes, livelihoods and farming because only a minor part of each holding was acquired. For the Wangliao Road in Yongchuan the affected people were paid RMB 36,000 per head in cash and a pension plan was bought for them paying RMB 500 a month per head with an annual increment, which the borrower says is much higher than their previous earnings from the land. The reported cost of land acquisition and resettlement is also given twice: the body text says the original estimate of US$50 million was much higher than the actual US$15 million, and Annex 7 says the final cost for compensation was around US$20 million at loan closing.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2017 rated Moderately Unsatisfactory by the Bank's own completion report and by its Independent Evaluation Group. The Tongliang land compensation was put on the correct basis only at the moment of closing, three years after the road works there were finished. The completion report's body text and its own Annex 7 give different figures for how much land was taken, how many square metres of housing were demolished, how many people were affected and what the compensation cost, and neither document reconciles them.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,912 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count: it looked for what Bank documents call project-affected people, searching them for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced"; where a document counted only households it looked up an average household size; it decided to include all impacts, temporary ones among them, and says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement plans written before the work was done. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.

cases.community: The project worked in 18 nationally designated poor counties in Guangxi, Sichuan and Yunnan, eleven of them ethnic minority autonomous counties, and built village access roads, health clinics, drinking water facilities and other village works. The completion report states that over 8,000 project households in Guangxi were affected by the acquisition of about 3,000 mu of land for the construction of village access roads, health clinics and drinking water facilities. Its account of how that land was obtained is favourable: most of the land needed for village-level works was voluntarily provided by the affected villages and villagers, the acquisition in Guangxi was carried out to the satisfaction of the affected people through participatory approaches, case study investigations suggest the affected people were satisfied with the arrangements and that their income levels rose by at least 50 per cent on average between 2004 and 2010, and all land acquisition was generally done in accordance with Chinese regulations and Bank policies. Against that the report records a finding by the Bank's own safeguards specialist: "agreement in writing was not always reached in advance with the PAPs when it was necessary to take their land in order to complete project civil works", and that compensation standards should be adequately discussed with and supported by the affected people and should be in line with local government regulations. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the point in its own words, that agreement on land acquisition in writing was not always timely in reaching the affected people and that compensation standards needed to be more adequately explained to them. The appraisal document had anticipated that land acquisition would be limited and scattered and that "no physical relocation of people is anticipated to be necessary", and the completion report records none. The report also records what made the land easier to obtain: the participatory approach, early advance notice and community mobilisation, with communities and villagers voluntarily offering land once they understood that they would be the direct beneficiaries of the roads, water facilities and clinics built on it.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2011 rated Satisfactory. Over 8,000 households in Guangxi had given up land, about 3,000 mu in all, and the Bank's safeguards specialist found that written agreement had not always been reached with them before the land was taken. The Independent Evaluation Group raised the risk to the development outcome to Significant and cut borrower performance to Moderately Satisfactory. Neither Bank document states what compensation those households received.

It drew mainly on resettlement plans written before the work was done. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.

cases.community: The resettlement plan prepared under the Bank-financed assessment identifies 289 households, a population of 2,048 making up 527 families, as project-affected people in the seven Stage 1 villages, on the basis of the 2011 census. All of them lose their house plots and their agricultural and pasture land. Among them, 38 household heads are women, three of those widows; 31 people are disabled, 22 men and 9 women; 23 household heads are disabled; and 12 households, 4.1 per cent, were found to be very poor. The plan records that resettlement at Rogun started more than 30 years ago, was interrupted by the civil war and resumed, and that it was decided not to interrupt the process for the Stage 1 villages, so moves continued while the plan was being written. A table of families already resettled as of June 2011 gives 20 at Rudaki against an intended 286, 70 at Dangara against 250, 100 at Tursunzade against 367, 35 at Darband against 15,000 and none at Chormagzak against 67; the plan notes that this table does not distinguish families from the Stage 1 and Stage 2 villages and gives no total. As of end September 2011, 24 families from Sicharog Jamoat in Rogun district had moved to the new sites. Of the Stage 1 villages, 230 graves had to be relocated. The plan's own household survey records the loss of fruit and timber trees as the main negative aspect of the move, followed by a lack of funds to build the new houses, then the loss of agricultural land, with 14 per cent of respondents reporting difficulties in moving and 10 per cent regretting leaving the place they were born; the main positive aspects given were a constant supply of electricity, the prospect of new jobs and better housing. The plan then sets out the main points of the Bureau for Human Rights report described below, beginning with the statement that in general the majority of the people are satisfied with the way resettlement is handled by the government organisations, and listing the complaints that report recorded. Valuation of most properties, mainly houses, was carried out in 2009 while compensation was paid later, when people started building at the new site, and prices for construction material and labour had risen in the meantime without the compensation amount taking that into account. Compensation was paid in stages beginning with 30 per cent when construction started, which caused problems for many households, who asked for payment in full or at least 70 per cent up front. Payment went only to the owner of the structure, as a rule the household head, although many households contained several families, so other families living with the owner had to build at their own expense. No special provisions were being made for households headed by women, for disabled or for elderly people. People living near the dam in the risk zone faced inconvenience and danger from construction. House plots of 1,000 square metres at the new sites were said to be insufficient for large households. Transport of movable assets to the new site was provided but was often not enough for all possessions, especially livestock, so many people had to sell some of their animals. Complaints were made about the information given and the chance to take part in decisions, and about water supply, road conditions and schools at the new sites. The plan adds that many of the relocated households mentioned the availability and fertility of agricultural land at the new sites at Tursunzade, Rudaki and Dangara, and that nobody complained of a lack of land or of access to it. An early resettlement audit found that compensation amounts needed updating to replacement cost and to account for inflation, that vulnerable groups needed special support with house construction, transport and livelihood restoration, that transport capacity for moving all movable assets including livestock was insufficient, and that a structure was needed on the ground to improve public participation; the plan says the Resettlement Unit had begun building those recommendations into its daily practice. The Dushanbe non-governmental organisation Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law, working under an EU assignment, evaluated the resettlement in parallel and its report is quoted at length in the Bank-disclosed plan: there is no independent property valuation institution in Tajikistan, most housing was assessed in 2009 and the assessed value was not enough to build decent housing by 2011, the staged 30 per cent payments left residents who had spent the first instalment unable to build and mostly unemployed, people lacked clear information on relocation and on how complaints would be handled, and some new areas still had no power lines, water supply, schools, kindergartens, medical facilities or roads despite a legal requirement to put those in before relocation; the same seven conclusions also state that in most cases people were willing to move and consented, while the oldest residents and people with disabilities wanted to stay where they were or move nearby. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 25 June 2014 from 156 interviews carried out between November 2013 and February 2014, states that the government resettled about 1,500 families from 2009 onward, that resettlement sites are often more than 100 km from the original villages and some families were moved as far as 200 km, that families said compensation was too low to replace their homes, that agricultural land was not available in all resettled communities, that families spent more on food and lost farming and livestock income, that some new communities had no school and children walked up to two hours to class, and that blasting near the site damaged homes.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,048 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Stage 1 Resettlement Action Plan states that a total of 289 households, whose population is 2,048, making up 527 families, were identified as project-affected people from the 2011 census. The plan's own table of families already resettled by June 2011 gives four site figures of 20, 70, 100 and 35, with none at a fifth site, and states that the table does not separate Stage 1 from Stage 2 families; the plan gives no total of people moved. Human Rights Watch puts the number resettled from 2009 onward at about 1,500 families, which covers the dam as a whole and not only Stage 1.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2014 having paid for the assessment studies and not for construction or resettlement. The Bank's completion report of 29 June 2015 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14942, posted 9 June 2016, gave outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Significant, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 27 July 2020 lowered those to outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, risk to development outcome High, Bank performance Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. That report also records that the Bank opted not to finance Rogun, that the assessment process helped the Government make the case for raising finance through Eurobonds in 2017 to start work on the dam, and that the first two of six planned turbines were launched by the end of 2019.

cases.conditions: The Independent Evaluation Group's review sets out the sequence: the appraisal document stated that the project 'would not trigger any Safeguards policies, since it would be implemented on existing electricity and gas networks' and classified it environmental category C, a classification the additional financing project paper repeats for the original project; the completion report recognises that the original project was in fact category B, because it involved installing electricity and gas meters in existing consuming centres; and under the additional financing the category was changed to A to reflect the potential impacts of the Rogun hydroelectric project for which the assessment studies were being carried out, which is the category the completion report's data sheet records. The completion report rates safeguards Satisfactory throughout and states that the recipient and the implementing agencies were in compliance with the agreed safeguard policies under both the original grant and the additional financing. A Resettlement Policy Framework was prepared alongside the Stage 1 plan, to be applied to Stage 2 resettlement, and a separate Resettlement Audit was commissioned to examine resettlement already done and to inform retroactive measures needed to bring it up to the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy. A three-step grievance procedure was set out in the plan; the practice at the time was a single-instance mechanism run by the Resettlement Unit, with a journal of complaints, named officials at each new site and a telephone line (Resettlement Action Plan for Stage 1, 28 August 2014; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 June 2015; ICR Review ICRR14942, 9 June 2016).

cases.title: Land Taken at Kwabenya for a Landfill That Was Never Built
cases.place: Kwabenya, Ga East, Greater Accra Region, Ghana
cases.point: Kwabenya, the suburb beside the proposed sanitary landfill site, where the Agyemankata community lives (OpenStreetMap suburb point, Ga East Municipal District)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit 3889-GH, written IDA-38890 in the completion report, of SDR 41.6 million for the Second Urban Environmental Sanitation Project (P082373). Approved 29 April 2004 and signed 13 August 2004. The dollar equivalent is given as US$62.0 million by the completion report and the Project Performance Assessment Report and as US$64.39 million by the Inspection Panel's investigation report. US$25.7 million was allocated to the solid waste management component, of which the Kwabenya sanitary landfill was a subcomponent with base costs estimated at US$9.5 million. Closing was extended from 30 June 2010 to 31 December 2012. The credit was restructured three times; the third restructuring, approved 18 December 2012, extended closing by seven months and added a new disbursement category, Compensation Payments to Project Affected Persons, so that credit proceeds could pay compensation under the Kwabenya plan. The project cost table records US$0.18 million actually spent on compensation against nothing at appraisal. The completion report of 27 June 2013 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14631, posted 20 April 2015, gave the same first three ratings and gave risk to development outcome as Significant. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 19 May 2016 reached the same four ratings as the review and does not rate safeguards. The implementing agencies were the metropolitan and municipal assemblies of the participating cities, coordinated by a Project Coordination Unit in the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development.

companies.name: Accra Metropolitan Assembly
companies.role: The local government authority for Accra, responsible under the Project Coordination Unit of the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development for the city's component of the project, including the Kwabenya landfill. It requested compensation claims to be lodged with the Executive Secretary of the Land Valuation Board, told the Bank in October 2010 through the Mayor of Accra to drop Kwabenya, and listed three years of non-payment of compensation among its reasons for discontinuing the landfill.

companies.name: Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development
companies.role: The ministry responsible for local government in Ghana. Its Project Coordination Unit coordinated the components implemented by the five participating metropolitan and municipal assemblies.

cases.community: The project was to build a sanitary landfill near the village of Kwabenya to serve greater Accra, which had an estimated load of 500,000 tonnes of refuse a year. The site had been chosen for an earlier British-funded landfill from 1999; that effort built an access road and a drainage culvert and was then dropped over land right claims, and the Panel and the Project Performance Assessment Report both record that after the access road was built people moved into the area and started economic activities near the site. The Government issued an Executive Instrument on 26 January 2007 compulsorily acquiring the land, which vests it in the President free of all encumbrances, with a six-month deadline to submit compensation claims. The Panel was informed that demolition markers were painted on structures in the community in the same month, and its report includes a picture captioned 'Houses marked for demolition by National Security Authority'. In July 2007 the authorities issued a notice that rights to compensation would be forfeited if claims were not submitted by the six-month deadline. The Panel's investigation report of 13 March 2009 found that the Bank did not comply with its policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and project supervision, on the analysis of alternative sites, the analysis of impacts in the project's area of influence, environmental management planning and resettlement planning. It found that land acquisition and compensation activities started before a resettlement action plan was prepared, contrary to the project's own Resettlement Policy Framework, and that management failed to ensure that affected people were given an information sheet in a language they could read setting out the purpose of the survey or explaining the resettlement and compensation procedures. It recorded that many of the people involved were poor women working as stone quarriers who were likely to lose their livelihoods to the land acquisition, migrants with uncertain legal entitlement to be in the country, and people treated as squatters and informal quarriers with no title or permit and no legal right to compensation under local law. No Bank social scientist visited the site between 2003 and the end of 2007, the period in which relations deteriorated, and no resettlement or social safeguard specialist joined a supervision mission until the mid-term review in December 2007. At the mid-term review in October 2010 the Government asked to drop the Kwabenya site and move the funds to other activities. In April 2012 the Government asked the Bank to use credit proceeds to pay compensation for the 76 inhabited structures identified in the draft plan, undertaking to pay for the land itself, and the closing date was extended seven months to 31 December 2012 to process the payments. The payments were not completed by that date; the completion report gives as reasons that some affected people refused compensation, apparently hoping to hold on to the land, and that some said the compensation offered did not reflect inflation and current market values. In June 2015 the Government told the Bank it would revoke the Executive Instrument on which the expropriation was based, which would restore the affected people's rights. The Panel's third and final progress report of 15 October 2015 concluded that action to complete the expropriation had stalled, that no compensation under the plan was accepted by the affected people and that some continued to build on the land, and that these actions reflected their intent to contest the expropriation and remain in place. A statement by the Agyemankata community annexed to the Bank's progress report of 29 August 2011 says that no notice was served before the Executive Instrument was published, that the Resettlement Policy Framework required compensation and resettlement before the confirming instrument was passed and this was not followed, and that 'our brothers and sisters of Agyemankata were given ten (10) days to leave their own homes without compensation. National Security gave the order.' The same statement says the Okaidja Gbeke family lodged compensation claims with the Land Valuation Board as the Accra Metropolitan Assembly required, on pain of forfeiting compensation, and had received no money and heard nothing, and it cites a Ghanaian Times report of 12 October 2009 headlined '35 Houses on G.A.E.C. Land demolished' in disputing an official statement that the land for the landfill site had been paid for.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 516 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, and the landfill was never built. The nearest figure in the Bank's documents is the 76 inhabited structures identified in the draft Resettlement Action Plan, which is a count of structures and not of people.
cases.suppression: Members of the community told the Panel during its eligibility visit that authorities came in January 2007 accompanied by 'armed policemen and national security' and marked their houses to be vacated, and that they had lost trust in the process. The Panel's own findings record that in September 2007 the Bank office and the Government agreed that work on the resettlement plan could proceed, despite the worsening safety situation, following the publication of the Executive Instrument in February 2007 and 'the marking of houses for possession in an operation supported by armed police'. The July 2007 notice that compensation rights would be forfeited if claims were not lodged by the deadline was seen by the requesters as a threat to their rights. The Panel also recorded Bank management's response, which quoted the Government's account that when officials delivered letters to members of the community in June 2004 inviting them to a meeting they 'were detained for several hours, confronted with death threats should they ever return, and the letters were returned unopened', and that since that incident government delegations, project staff, surveyors and valuation staff had visited the site under the protection of armed security personnel. The Panel found that the Bank and the Government tried to consult a broad spectrum of potentially affected people but failed to reach the Agyemankata group, which would not attend public hearings.
cases.outcome: The landfill was dropped at the mid-term review in October 2010 and the money moved to other activities, including landfills at Tema and Sekondi-Takoradi. The credit closed on 31 December 2012 with the compensation unpaid. In June 2015 the Government said it would revoke the Executive Instrument, restoring the affected people's rights, and the Bank treated that as resolving the requesters' concerns and the outstanding item in the management action plan. The Panel issued its third and final progress report on 15 October 2015. The Bank told the Independent Evaluation Group that it would keep following up with the Government on enacting the cancellation and would issue a final note.
