cx: Ghana: Second Urban Environmental Sanitation Project (P082373)
cases.conditions: The project was a repeater of the first Urban Environmental Sanitation Project and used that project's streamlined procedures, although the first project did not include the Kwabenya landfill. The environmental and social assessment for the landfill used the 1999 British-financed environmental assessment as its basis; management acknowledged that at the time of that assessment there were 'virtually no resettlement needs' and that people moved closer to the site after the access road was built. A Resettlement Policy Framework was reviewed at appraisal and found by management to be in line with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, while the Bank's own Quality at Entry Assessment called it 'somewhat disorganized, unfocused, vague and repetitive, and insufficiently operational' and said the team appeared to have underestimated the grounds of remaining objections at Kwabenya. The Development Credit Agreement required a detailed resettlement action plan acceptable to the Bank, and the obligation to compensate affected people in accordance with Bank policy survived the abandonment of the landfill and the closing of the project, as did the Bank's supervision obligations. The framework itself provided that compensation and resettlement should be carried out before the confirming instrument on the land acquisition was passed; the Panel found that sequencing was not followed. The Bank insisted that compensation be paid only after the resettlement action plan was completed and accepted and, according to the Accra Metropolitan Assembly's own note, later said the environmental impact assessment should be completed before payment (Project Appraisal Document, 5 April 2004; Inspection Panel Investigation Report, 13 March 2009; Progress Report to the Board, 29 August 2011; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2013).

cases.title: Land Expropriated for the Road 19 Dual Carriageway
cases.place: National Road 19 between Santo Tome and the Cordoba provincial boundary, Departamento Las Colonias, Province of Santa Fe, Argentina
cases.point: Franck, Departamento Las Colonias, the town the two people who signed the 2007 Request for Inspection live in (OpenStreetMap place point for the Municipio de Franck)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan 7429-AR of US$126.7 million to the Province of Santa Fe for the Santa Fe Road Infrastructure Project (P099051), guaranteed by the Argentine Republic, approved 13 February 2007, with the loan and guarantee agreements signed 12 June 2007. Closing was 30 June 2012, the original date. The completion report's financing table puts the province's contribution at US$46.4 million at appraisal and US$49.8 million in the event. The Inspection Panel's investigation report gives the total project cost as about US$173.1 million and the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives US$173.10 million at appraisal and US$176.50 million actual; the completion report's cost annex gives total project costs of US$126.70 million at appraisal and US$126.4 million actual, the figure its financing table records as the Bank loan, with resettlement entered as zero in both columns. The loan paid to upgrade 130 km of Road 19 in Santa Fe into a four-lane highway; the remaining 6 km in Cordoba were funded by the National Road Directorate. The province was to expropriate land to reach a right of way of 120 metres. The completion report of 24 June 2013 rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14284, posted 24 March 2014, agreed on outcome, risk to development outcome and borrower performance and gave overall Bank performance as Moderately Satisfactory, noting that the environmental and social management plan was not fully in compliance.

companies.name: Direccion Provincial de Vialidad, Province of Santa Fe
companies.role: The provincial roads directorate of Santa Fe, which carried out the expropriations and the land and structure valuations. Its staff visited landowners, and the Project Implementation Unit inside it ran the Resettlement and Expropriation Plan and reported monthly to the Bank's task team leader.

companies.name: Direccion Nacional de Vialidad
companies.role: Argentina's national roads directorate, which funded the 6 km of Road 19 inside Cordoba province and had carried out 69 expropriations along the same road in 1972; encroachments on that earlier right of way were notified to it and to the contractor in the second half of 2008.

cases.community: The project widened 136 km of Road 19 between Santo Tome in Santa Fe and San Francisco in Cordoba, 130 km of it with Bank money, by building a second carriageway and taking land to reach a 120-metre right of way. The completion report states that 246 parcels were expropriated. The province's own completion report, summarised in the annexes of the Bank's, breaks those down into 208, or 84 per cent, taken by agreement, 33, or 14 per cent, through the courts, 2, or 0.8 per cent, state land, and 3, or 1.2 per cent, in the end not affected. Twenty additional expropriations were identified during the works and were almost finished at project closure. The report also records that 17 cases of families in vulnerable socio-economic conditions were dealt with, and that the programme to maintain the socio-economic conditions of the 26 families and economic units on expropriated parcels was completed towards the end of 2009, with the Project Management Unit monitoring cases into early 2010. School No. 1303, General Jose de San Martin, at San Agustin, stood inside the right of way; it was rebuilt with provincial funds and was operating in March 2010. The access road to Agro-Technical School No. 299 was paved for 2.5 km, finished in mid-2011, to offset the taking of part of that school's land. Two residents of Franck submitted a Request for Inspection on 7 September 2007 on their own behalf and on behalf of ten other residents who signed it, over the road's drainage design and flood risk, the amount of land taken and the compensation for it, and the consultation process; they also raised discrimination and intimidation in the land acquisition process. The Panel's investigation report of 2 July 2008 found that the Resettlement Action Plan complied with the involuntary resettlement policy for the 26 cases where more than 40 per cent of the land was taken or where there were improvements on it, because those were analysed in depth and given a socio-economic restoration programme. For properties where less than 40 per cent was taken and there were no improvements, the plan gathered only cadastral and land use data; the Panel was not shown evidence that a policy-consistent socio-economic analysis of the impact of losing a fraction of land was prepared, nor that consultations with those landowners during preparation sufficiently addressed the negative effects of partial expropriation, and it found that the lack of a complete socio-economic analysis covering all people affected by land acquisition was not consistent with the policy. The Panel went on to find that although there was only partial compliance with that policy at the start, communication with landowners improved significantly during implementation, some measures to address the effects of the partial taking were provided for, and the project was by then in compliance with it. Bank staff told the Panel that partial expropriation was compensated even though no detailed socio-economic study was carried out, that landowners were offered expropriation of the whole property where the remainder would no longer be economically viable, and that owners outside the restoration programme were offered technical advice, information on provincial productive projects and help coordinating with local business; the Panel learned that some of this was offered only recently, after social and communication experts were added to the Project Implementation Unit. The Panel heard complaints from requesters and others that pressure had been applied to accept compensation offers they considered below market value, and in other cases that owners had not been visited and had only received written notice. Other affected people said they were discriminated against because the value offered for their land was lower than for neighbouring land; management acknowledged that the soil classification maps which could have explained different values on adjoining holdings were not shared with landowners, which the Panel found generated perceptions of unfairness. One person told the Panel that a number of elderly people, including his own father, had accepted what he considered low offers because they feared being taken to court if they refused. Opinions among affected people differed: one said a counter-offer won him improved compensation, and another said that talking to others along the right of way helped them collectively judge market value and get reasonable compensation. At the time of the Panel's visit the Project Implementation Unit said 195 cash compensation agreements had been signed, 34 were under judicial review, two properties were state-owned schools, one was no longer affected because the road was changed, and 13 cases were still being processed. On the flooding claims, the Panel found the assessment of effects upstream of the road appropriate but found the Bank in non-compliance on downstream flooding, and considered that the methodologies the engineering firms used were not homogeneous and that the evidence did not support a conclusion that the upgrade would not harm affected people. A further study was commissioned in November 2009 under the management action plan. The completion report states that studies verified the adequacy of the designs but did so at the limit of capacity, so that drainage could collapse if rainfall exceeded the levels seen in March 2007, and that additional drainage works were added at Los Cuatro Sauces, Canada del Sauce and Arroyo del Sauce. Residents submitted a fourth Request for Inspection in September 2011, which the Panel did not register because implementation was almost complete with disbursements above 95 per cent; the Project Management Unit agreed to add measures to address the residents' perception of risk.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 305 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The counts in the Bank's own documents are of parcels and cases: 246 parcels expropriated, 26 families and economic units in the socio-economic restoration programme, 17 cases of families in vulnerable conditions dealt with, and one school rebuilt.
cases.suppression: The requesters alleged discrimination and intimidating notices during the expropriation process. The Panel did not find any evidence of intimidating notices having been sent to landowners, and said the only written communication it saw was a sample letter of 26 December 2006 sent by the Project Implementation Unit to everyone whose land was to be expropriated, telling them they would be visited and pointing them to the plan on the website. The Panel did find it possible that some landowners were not given sufficient opportunity to consider their options and may have felt pressured into accepting offers. Bank management said it took any allegation of discrimination and intimidation very seriously and would follow up closely. The Project Implementation Unit told the Panel that checks existed inside the provincial roads directorate, including an audit by the Tribunal de Cuentas each time a payment was approved, that all affected people had been told about an appeal route through the provincial ombudsman, and that the ombudsman had received no complaints. Bank staff in Washington sampled five case files at the directorate and found no evidence that expropriation and valuation procedures had not been followed.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2012 on its original date. The completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory and records recurrent conflict over land valuations, with owners putting very high values on their land as commodity prices rose, and says the province tried where it could to compensate owners further through complementary works such as improved accesses and small infrastructure. The Panel's investigation found the Bank in non-compliance on downstream flood assessment and on information given during land acquisition, and found that information sharing and consultation improved over time; it recorded that some requesters told it the expropriation process eventually concluded to their satisfaction. A management action plan was carried out and a progress report went to the Board on 14 June 2010.

cases.conditions: The project was prepared with a detailed environmental and social management plan and a Resettlement and Expropriation Plan. The province was to expropriate land to reach a right of way of 120 metres, under provincial legislation that allowed a landowner to have the whole property expropriated where a partial taking left the remainder economically unviable. Bank staff worked with the Project Implementation Unit to build a matrix tracking the expropriation of every property, which the unit updated and Bank staff reviewed on periodic visits, and the unit sent the task team leader a monthly report on implementation of the plan. Affected people were told of an appeal route through the provincial ombudsman's office, and each compensation payment was audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas when approved (Inspection Panel Investigation Report, 2 July 2008; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 June 2013).

cases.community: The project built bus corridors and bus rapid transit systems in several Indian cities. The completion report states that land acquisition took 75 hectares of private land, affecting more than 11,000 landowners, and physically displaced 425 families, and that about 500 tenants and informal settlers were also affected. At appraisal, impacts had been envisaged for only about 1,200 people in Pimpri-Chinchwad. In Pimpri-Chinchwad the project took private land from more than 10,000 landowners and displaced 400 families, 144 of them informal settlers. The report lists the difficulties there as inordinate delays in resettlement, delays in payment of compensation, prolonged court cases, a longer stay of displaced families in a transit camp, and delays in handing land to contractors. Compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy at that subproject was rated Unsatisfactory or Moderately Unsatisfactory for three years, from July 2015 to March 2018, because of non-compliance with payment of compensation and delays in shifting displaced families. Compensation for about 80 per cent of the 10,000 affected landowners was deposited in the courts for want of ownership documents. In Hubli-Dharwad the project acquired 30 acres affecting 1,043 landowners and 500 tenants and informal settlers and displaced 21 families; the report names compensation rates for private land, resistance from religious trustees to relocating affected places of worship, and compensation for road margin areas as the key difficulties, and calls the relocation of affected workshop premises one of the hardest parts. In Naya Raipur four displaced families were given alternative housing under a government scheme and three affected small shopkeepers were given shops on a rental basis. The report also records that the project brought more than 700 untitled holders into resettlement assistance who would otherwise have been left out, and that 110 households were given security of tenure to their resettled homes in Pimpri-Chinchwad. At the time the completion report was written, compensation was still owed to 7 landowners and resettlement to 9 informal families in Pimpri-Chinchwad, and compensation to 33 landowners and resettlement assistance to 7 tenants in Hubli-Dharwad; the report attributes those delays to the people concerned not being available to receive compensation or to a lack of ownership documents, and concludes that compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy 'was met with prolonged delays'. The Independent Evaluation Group records a later position given to it by the project team in May 2019: in Pimpri-Chinchwad compensation was pending for 5 landowners out of 230 for want of ownership documents and allotment of alternative houses was pending for 5 families out of 401; in Hubli compensation had been paid to all landowners except 131 out of 1,043, who had refused the offer and gone to court for a review, with their compensation deposited in court; and resettlement assistance for 8 tenants out of about 500 was no longer needed because the corridor was finished inside the existing right of way. Those figures were attributed to the project team, not to a document, and the landowner totals they use for Pimpri-Chinchwad differ from the more than 10,000 in the completion report.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-44550 of SDR 115.4 million (US$190 million equivalent) and Credit IDA-51850 of SDR 64.9 million (US$100 million equivalent) for the Second Central Transport Corridor Project (P103633), the second credit being the additional financing approved 15 January 2013 and carried under its own number P124114. The project financed Phase 1 of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system and work at Tanzanian airports. The Government of Tanzania was to finance resettlement, entered in the completion report's cost and financing tables at US$10.7 million both at appraisal and at the additional financing, of which US$10.3 million, 96.2 per cent, was spent; a footnote elsewhere in the same report gives the Government's resettlement contribution as US$10.0 million. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, with quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory and quality of supervision Moderately Satisfactory, and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021021 recorded the same ratings with no disagreement and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial. The implementing agencies were the Dar Rapid Transit Agency and the Tanzania National Roads Agency.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency
companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which held fiduciary oversight of the project and ran the works contracts. The completion report says the census of project-affected people and property valuation were done before contractors were engaged, and that the agency's own account credits the Bank's local office with a leadership role among donors.

companies.name: Dar Rapid Transit Agency
companies.role: The government agency set up to deliver and oversee the bus rapid transit system in Dar es Salaam, named in the completion report as an implementing agency alongside the roads agency.

cases.community: The project built the first phase of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system, which required a terminal at Kariakoo and a bus depot at Ubungo. The completion report states that the total number of project-affected people was 877 at the start and later rose to 1,236, and that the actual resettlement plan budget was TZS 23.5 billion, about US$11 million. Serious problems emerged with compensation. In January 2011, on an implementation support mission, the Bank team learned that insufficient funds had been allocated to meet the commitments under the resettlement plan. The inadequate funding and legal disputes, including a court injunction, led to contractual disputes and the termination of two works contracts, for the Kariakoo terminal and the Ubungo depot, because the sites were not available to the contractors. Two feeder transfer stations were not acquired at all and the operational design had to be changed. The plan was updated in March 2012 and the Ministry of Finance increased the money available, and the Government introduced a communications outreach strategy and set up a grievance redress mechanism. The people affected at the Kariakoo terminal site had filed a court case in 2008 and obtained an injunction blocking the Government from accessing the site. The completion report states that the site, with 106 families in semidetached buildings, was nonetheless cleared by the Government in March 2012 after the High Court dismissed their application for an injunction on technical grounds. They filed a separate civil suit and sought a further injunction, and in December 2013 the High Court ruled formally releasing the site to the Government for public use as the terminal, while the main suit was still pending judgment. The report records that the main case was still pending judgment in 2017, eight years after it was filed. It also states that the compensation funds were deposited in an escrow account and that most of the affected people had already claimed their compensation, and that a Tanzanian practising lawyer attended the court hearings as an observer for the Bank. The report says insufficient funding was set aside for the costs of compensation and relocation of project-affected people. Phase 1 of the system was expected to displace 1,800 existing minibuses, known as daladala, whose owners were to be compensated through preferential access to bus rapid transit routes and through payment for scrapped vehicles; the report says only a fraction of the daladala had been displaced as of end-2016. After initial construction, flash flooding occurred at Jangwani along the Msimbazi river basin, which analysis attributed to rapid siltation of the basin from uncontrolled encroachment, solid waste and human activity upstream; flood prevention measures were taken, and a more permanent solution involving the relocation of petty traders was left to later phases.

cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,862 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. cases.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2016, five years after the original date. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on both. The main court case brought by the people cleared from the Kariakoo site in 2008 was still awaiting judgment when the report was written in 2017; their compensation had been placed in escrow and the report says most of the affected people had claimed it. The report says that for later phases of the system the compensation resources are to be in place before works begin, and draws the lesson that adequate preparation of resettlement is a critical requirement.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit 5140-KE, written IDA-51400, for the Kenya National Urban Transport Improvement Project (P126321). US$300 million at approval, revised to US$92.53 million (SDR 43.96 million), of which US$61.87 million was disbursed, 22.7 per cent of the original credit. Approved 2 August 2012, effective 24 December 2012, closed 31 December 2018 on its scheduled date. On 21 December 2018, at the Government's request, the undisbursed balance of XDR 149.5 million, US$207.5 million equivalent at that date, was cancelled; the Bank told the Government so by letter of 27 December 2018. The Bank had raised implementation problems in letters and aide memoires in December 2016, August 2017, January 2018 and August 2018 and in meetings on 11 December 2018. The completion report names delays and shortfalls in Government counterpart funding, particularly for compensation for project-affected persons and for relocating services, among the causes. The project was reclassified from environmental category B to category A because incorporating bus rapid transit into the James Gichuru junction to Rironi section required wider resettlement areas and land acquisition, which the report describes as resulting in significant, large scale and irreversible adverse environmental and social impacts; the updated safeguards data sheet was disclosed on 9 November 2018 but the restructuring was never finalised. companies.role: The state corporation responsible for Kenya's national trunk roads, which ran the James Gichuru junction to Rironi works and the resettlement plans for them. cases.community: The project widened the A104 from the James Gichuru junction in Nairobi to Rironi in Kiambu County and built bypasses at Kisumu and Meru. The second update of the resettlement plan for the James Gichuru junction to Rironi section identified 5,181 project-affected persons, 3,364 structures and 839 parcels of land, against 1,322 affected persons, 133 structures and no land acquisition identified at appraisal for the whole A104 corridor programme. The estimated cost of carrying out that plan rose from US$1.3 million to US$120 million by project completion. The completion report sets out the position on payments as at 25 April 2019. On the James Gichuru to Rironi section, sub-lot 3C had 808 affected persons of whom 133 had been paid, with KES 1,037,554,915.74 due, KES 724,124,449.47 paid and KES 313,430,466.27 outstanding; Lots 3A and 3B were still under valuation by the National Land Commission at closure. On the Kisumu Northern bypass, 507 affected persons of whom 299 had been paid, with KES 947,034,632 due, KES 277,242,405 paid and KES 669,792,227 outstanding. On the Meru bypass, 921 affected persons of whom 890 had been paid, with KES 775,149,522.94 due, KES 755,815,684.94 paid and KES 19,333,838.00 outstanding; the report says compensation there was complete apart from people with succession issues. Affected people on the James Gichuru to Rironi section petitioned the Bank on 13 December 2018 alleging delay in payment for land acquisition and the associated compensation, and raising health and safety, dust emissions, access to homes and businesses, and restoration of community water connections; a Bank team met their representatives on 19 December 2018 at their request. A fatal incident occurred on 5 October 2017 on the James Gichuru to Rironi section, which the completion report attributes to inadequate traffic management at the construction site; gaps were identified from the investigation and an action plan was prepared and carried out, but compensation to the family of the person killed had not been paid by project closure because the case was pending before the magistrate's court at Limuru. There were allegations of eviction of affected people during the works, which the roads authority denied by letter of 8 April 2019, stating that 'there has been No Eviction of Project Affected Person without compensation whatsoever.' A petition to preserve Sigona House, which the applicants said had historical and architectural value, was lodged in the High Court of Kenya; the National Museums of Kenya decided the building did not qualify as a structure of historical importance under national guidelines, and the roads authority redesigned the service road to avoid it. The Star reported on 31 May 2019 that residents and business owners along the route, organised as People Affected by the Project under its chairman Kimani Njuki, wanted the expansion halted until those affected were compensated; that houses had been marked for demolition and tenants had moved out; that supermarkets, petrol stations, hotels and shops had closed, among them a Rironi petrol station closed by Peter Mwaura of Pekangu Enterprises; and that Issac Kahura was struggling to repay a loan on two flats after his tenants left. The group had complained to the Senate and to the national human rights commission, and the Transport Cabinet Secretary had missed three Senate committee invitations, on 9, 21 and 30 May 2019. The same paper reported on 20 August 2019 that Infrastructure Principal Secretary Julius Korir said KES 12 billion was needed to pay for land and structures, that the 25 km stretch was 40 per cent complete and had stalled over the money to pay property owners, that work had continued from Gitaru to Rironi after landowners were paid KES 1.2 billion, and that the section between Gitaru and ABC was undone because of non-compensation.

companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which implemented the road component and held fiduciary responsibility for the project, and which hired three additional procurement staff for it.

cases.community: The project paved and improved runways, taxiways, aprons and terminals at Bukoba, Kigoma, Tabora and Zanzibar airports and rehabilitated road lengths. The completion report rates the project's social safeguard management satisfactory. It states that resettlement plans were prepared for all the airports, that no resettlement was required at Tabora or Kigoma, that resettlement at Zanzibar airport was completed, and that at Bukoba five resettlement cases remained pending at project closure. Four of those five were awaiting court deliberations. The fifth had been resolved through the project's grievance redress mechanism, with the entitlement agreed and payment still pending from the Tanzania Airports Authority. The authority agreed to keep submitting progress reports to the Bank until the remaining cases were resolved. During implementation it was found that Tumaini Primary School, a public primary school serving the area around Bukoba airport and hosting a unit for more than 50 disabled children, stood within the flight path of the extended runway. Flight restrictions were imposed so that operations were allowed only in the direction away from the school, and it was decided that the school had to be relocated. Empty land was contributed by the local government, new school buildings were put up, and both former and new students began attending in the new location; the original school was demolished and its land demarcated. The completion report says there were some students whose commute was made more challenging but that the move was largely successful, and that the airports authority and the Bukoba airport management committed to continue supporting the school. On the road component, the lengths were built inside existing alignments and no resettlement was found to be required; the 7 km stretch of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was left out of the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been needed there, although the detailed designs for it were finished. During implementation several families living near a quarry used by the Arusha to Minjingo contractor asked to be relocated; the report says their request was met and they were relocated. At Zanzibar airport the extension of the taxiway required a cemetery to be relocated, which the report says was done satisfactorily. No archaeologist was engaged as the project had expected, although the report says very little undisturbed land was used and no chance finds were identified.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,595 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The only figures in the Bank's documents are five resettlement cases still pending at Bukoba at project closure, four of them in court, and several unnumbered families near a quarry on the Arusha to Minjingo road who asked to be relocated and were.
cases.outcome: The credits closed on 20 June 2017, two years after the original closing date. Five resettlement cases at Bukoba were still unresolved at closure, four of them before the courts and one with payment outstanding. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team subsequently told it that the high court cases on carrying out the resettlement plan had been ruled on and that payment of compensation to the affected people was being processed; that statement is attributed to the project team and not to a document. The completion report of 16 January 2018 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

No independent source on the Bukoba resettlement cases or the school was found. The documents give no count of people, name nobody, do not say how much the outstanding entitlement was or what the four court cases were about, and do not say how many students' journeys to school became longer. The later statement that the court cases had been decided and payment was being processed is attributed to the project team rather than to a document. The completion report's cover page is dated January 16, 2017, five months before the closing date of 20 June 2017 that its own data sheet gives; the Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the date on the front page should be 2018 and not 2017, and the report's exchange rate is given as effective 27 December 2017.
cases.conditions: The project triggered Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11). Resettlement action plans were prepared for every airport in the project. The 7 km of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was deliberately excluded from the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been required there, while the detailed designs for a later rehabilitation were completed. The project was expected to engage an archaeologist to assess chance finds under the cultural property policy and did not do so. Construction companies were required to put in place HIV prevention education and sensitisation plans, including voluntary testing, in collaboration with district health officers (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 16 January 2018; ICR Review ICRR0021116, 25 May 2018).

fields_add.community: The Bank's own completion report of 13 February 2018 on the grant, IDA-H6990 of XDR 32.8 million or US$52 million equivalent, records that the project's involuntary resettlement compliance rating was Satisfactory at the start, was downgraded to Highly Unsatisfactory at the mid-term review, which brought the overall project rating down with it, and stood at Moderately Unsatisfactory at closing, the report recording that by the close of the project the rating was progressively upgraded from Highly Unsatisfactory to Unsatisfactory to Moderately Unsatisfactory, largely because of improvements in carrying out the Aynak plan, with better documentation of grievance intake, discrepancies in the names of project-affected persons clarified and a stronger understanding of the use of community organisers. The downgrade was based on the Ministry of Mines and Petroleum's slow and faltering implementation of the Aynak Resettlement Action Plan, its failure to observe the policies and procedures set out in that plan and in the project's Environmental and Social Management Framework as reflected in the financing agreement, poor handling of grievance redress and of reporting and documentation, and slow re-staffing of the Ministry's Social Adviser post. The report states that the information given to the Bank on resettlement was 'sparse and confusing', with limited connection between the plan and the project-affected persons named in it. The same passage records that, on the Ministry's own report, it had gone ahead with land acquisition and compensation for an access road close to the mine site without following due process: no household survey, no identification of losses and no second resettlement plan. Two deficiencies were still open at closing: the Ministry could not procure a water pump for the new township and resettlement site, which the report calls a barrier to completing the resettlement, and there was no agreement on the final list of people entitled to the various levels of compensation. A footnote to the same section says the Bank's safeguard procedures were simply not aligned with government laws, rules and procedures on land acquisition, and that where possible the laws and regulations were circumvented through a presidential decree, which took enormous effort and time and was not always within the control of the Aynak authority. At closing the Bank team was still seeking clarification from the land authority ARAZI on how it classified the categories of people eligible for compensation at Aynak.
fields_add.outcome: A project preparation grant attached to a later Bank operation took over responsibility for carrying out the Mes Aynak resettlement plan.

lenders_add.role: The parent project for the Bukavu-Goma works was the High Priority Reopening and Maintenance Project, Pro-Routes (P101745), approved 18 March 2008 and effective 7 October 2008, with a mid-term review on 19 March 2012 and closing extended from 30 September 2013 to 30 June 2020. It was financed by IDA Grant H359-DRC of SDR 32 million (US$50 million equivalent), IDA Grant H750-ZR of SDR 40 million (US$63.3 million equivalent) and Credit 5763-ZR of SDR 91.1 million (US$125 million equivalent), together with trust funds TF-92300 and TF-99492. World Bank financing was US$357.3 million at approval, revised to US$320.69 million, of which US$315.78 million was disbursed. Total project cost was US$429.92 million at approval, which included US$72.62 million from the UK Department for International Development; that financier disbursed nothing, and the revised and actual project cost figures are the World Bank's amounts alone. The project was environmental category A and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forests, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. The completion report of 21 June 2021 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022813 agreed on outcome, Bank performance and monitoring and evaluation, rated quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory, rated the quality of the completion report Substantial, and said there is high risk to the development outcome because it is not clear whether adequate resources will be allocated to maintain the roads reopened under the project.

fields_add.community: The second additional financing that paid for the Sake-Kavumu section was part of a project that ran from 18 March 2008 to 30 June 2020 and covered national roads well beyond the Bukavu-Goma road, among them stretches of RN4, RN5 and RN6 and the Kisangani to Banalia and Akula to Zongo axes. The parent project's completion report of 21 June 2021 states that 3,887 affected people were compensated across the project as a whole, that 2,891 claims were made through 157 local grievance mechanisms with 602 people put in place to run them, and that 1,416 of those claims were found to be legitimate and were settled to the satisfaction of the affected party. The report gives no account of the remaining claims. At least 30 safeguard instruments were prepared over the project's life, and more than 20 environmental and social management plans for work sites were prepared and carried out by contractors and the road agency's own crews. The project was designed to engage a non-governmental organisation to monitor and supervise compliance with the Bank's safeguard policies; over twelve years that role passed through five successive partners, including international consulting firms, and the report says the turnover contributed to the mismanagement of safeguards. The completion report also states that the Government complied with the management action plan following the Panel's recommendations.
fields_add.outcome: The parent project closed on 30 June 2020. Its completion report of 21 June 2021 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed, while rating the quality of Bank supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory.
